Iowa 7th Graders Reject Opportunity To Win Scholarship For Writing About Hemp –
"They objected to the marijuana leaf."

Drug fears kill scholarship
(Ed. note: There is a great irony in the double meaning of the headline. "Drug fears" did indeed kill scholarship. In fact, they prevented any critical thinking, just as intended.)

Essentially saying that drugs and education do not mix,

But school district administrators say the ultimate decision to reject the proposal from Alterna, a hemp-based beauty products manufacturer, came from the students.

"We let the kids know through our team leaders about it, and there was not even a hint that someone would want to participate,"

"The scholarship would be a nice thing. If it progressed at the usual rate, it might have become $8,000. But the core group of about 28 kids took a very active stance against it. The students said, ‘No, we fought so hard on this issue.’"

Alterna spokeswoman Kimberlee Jensen-Mitchell said the topic was not meant to advocate drug usage. In fact, she said, there is a requirement that no pro-drug essays be submitted.
(Ed. note: Would an essay arguing against marijuana prohibition have been pro-drug?)
Hemp is a form of the cannabis plant that contains very little THC, the active ingredient in marijuana that makes it psychoactive, she said. The plant has a variety of uses, including textile manufacture, beauty products and paper goods.

"I couldn’t change the topic," she said. "First of all, the topic is hemp. That is what’s controversial. That is what the controversial ingredient is in our hair-care line. It is a completely misunderstood substance. It is my job to dispel the myths and misinformation. Changing the topic would totally go against what I’m trying to do."

Burrus said he told Moline-Coal Valley Superintendent Ben McAdams about the sixth-graders’ disinterest. McAdams then turned down a $2,500 scholarship, proposed in August by Alterna, which is based in Los Angeles and owned by Moline native Don Christal. Alterna representatives had contacted McAdams, as well as Burrus, the district’s Parent Teacher Association, the Moline DARE officer, Police Chief Steve Etheridge and Mayor Stan Leach to ask their cooperation in a project they titled "Learn More."

The project would have featured an essay contest about hemp, an ingredient in some Alterna products. The winning essayist would have received a $2,500 scholarship invested in a trust until reaching college age. The winner would have been announced Dec. 1.

The idea for the scholarship, Jensen-Mitchell said, was based on the initiative taken in March by a class of sixth-graders at Ericsson Elementary School in Moline.

It was then that Ericsson School teacher Virginia Diamond wrote Ragan Outdoor Advertising (now Lamar), requesting that the company remove a billboard located on 5th Avenue adjacent to the school. The billboard was an advertisement for Alterna Hemp Shampoo, a product with hemp oil as an ingredient. Prominently featured in the billboard was a hemp leaf -- which is identical to a marijuana leaf.

"(They had) been studying advertising and how the media affects us," Diamond said. "They saw the billboard, which was right across the street, and felt a lot of little kids, kindergartners and first-graders, would only see the marijuana leaf and not see the shampoo bottle."
(Ed. note: I’ll bet they don’t study about how prohibitionist propaganda affects them! But they will figure that out in a few years.)

The billboard—one of eight in the Quad-City area—was part of a national advertising campaign concentrated primarily in the southwestern United States. Alterna moved the sign several blocks away as a result of the children’s letters.

"We are still prepared to offer the scholarship," Jensen-Mitchell said. "It’s just unfortunate that we are not going to offer it in Moline, especially since the idea of the scholarship came about because of the students at Ericsson."

She said the scholarship will be made available to students in California.
